text:
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- The Miami Dolphins are hopeful quarterback Malik Willis will return this season after his mandated minimum four-game stay on injured reserve, coach Jeff Hafley said Wednesday, and Willis is expected to remain the team's starter upon his return.

Hafley said Willis' MRI showed his groin injury had progressed to his core and the Dolphins' medical team believed he "needed the rest." Willis will seek a second opinion on his injury this week to decide whether or not to undergo surgery, but the Dolphins still see him as their starter, regardless of when he returns.

"Our hope is that he'll be back after his four weeks, which in time, if healthy, he'll return," Hafley said. "But he will be the starter when healthy, when he does return. And again, you look back at Malik and you watch him in that last game and you could see it. He couldn't quite move the way he had done early in the year and he was gritting through it and he was toughing through it. He made some plays with his feet in that game to keep plays alive.

"But we want him to be healthy so he can play at a high level without risking further injury."

Willis received treatment on his groin in each of the past two weeks. It didn't limit his practice participation, but he was noticeably hobbled in last week's loss to the Detroit Lions and was held to single-digit rushing yards for the second game in a row.

With Willis sidelined, second-year quarterback Kyle McCord will get his first career start Sunday against the Indianapolis Colts.

The Dolphins traded for McCord from the Green Bay Packers in August after the former sixth-round pick led the NFL in passing touchdowns this preseason. Though McCord has primarily run the Dolphins' scout team at practice since his arrival, Hafley said McCord's preseason tape showed desirable traits.

"He's got a strong arm, stronger than you think. He sees it well. The ball comes out fast," Hafley said. "He's decisive. He's aggressive. ... Again, he does not have experience in this league and this league is very different, but he does have experience. He has played in a lot of games, but from when I watched him, he's thrown a lot of passes and he does have arm talent and the ball comes out quickly and it'll be interesting to see."

The Philadelphia Eagles took McCord in the sixth round of the 2025 NFL draft, after he threw for an FBS-leading 4,779 yards at Syracuse as a senior. He also spent three seasons at Ohio State, going 11-1 as a starter in 2023.

McCord said it is his big-game experience in college that gives him confidence heading into the biggest week of his NFL career to date.

"It's a blessing, but I think once you get the first play, put on the helmet and get going, I think it'll feel just like football," McCord said of his opportunity. "And I feel like ... that's something that having played those big college games, I think you've been in those moments before my first time playing in a big game. I feel like that's where I'm drawing a lot of confidence from."

McCord said that despite his brief time in Miami, he has a full grasp of the playbook and can run "anything [offensive coordinator] Bobby [Slowik] wants to call." According to teammates, he has already shown that grasp at practice this week.

Right tackle Austin Jackson said McCord wasn't afraid to correct his teammates at Wednesday's practice, specifically when they weren't lined up appropriately.

"I would say he seemed pretty confident today in the huddle, calling the huddle, pretty confident calling the plays out," Jackson said. "There's a couple times the formation was wrong and he actually spotted it out beforehand, which is good. That's something that is big for a quarterback ... the confidence there is the main thing really, at the end of the day, that gets [a quarterback] through it."

Left tackle Patrick Paul said McCord has a "moxie" to him that he's excited for people to see Sunday and said he wasn't surprised by his practice habits "because he's a smart player."

Paul also said Miami's offensive line has a responsibility to ensure McCord remains comfortable during his first start.

"As the O-line, you have to make him feel comfortable," Paul said. "So that's setting a firm pocket and then just off the field, getting with him, talking with him, making sure he's confident, and then just praising him when you can -- just letting him know that you're there and supporting him."

text:
Colts wide receiver Alec Pierce remains in rehab for a heel injury with no set timeline for his return.

Pierce reaggravated the injury in Week 2 after undergoing surgery in late March.

The Colts recently traded their top two healthy receivers, Josh Downs and Keenan Allen.

Despite playing only five quarters, Pierce is still among the team's top three wideouts in catches and yards.

INDIANAPOLIS – Colts lead wide receiver Alec Pierce remains in rehab seven weeks after reaggravating his surgically repaired left heel early in the Colts’ Week 2 road loss to the Chiefs, Colts head coach Shane Steichen said Wednesday. Steichen declined to give a timeline on a possible return for Pierce or commit to the return of the team’s top receiver at all.

Pierce missed nearly all of the Colts’ offseason workout programs after undergoing surgery on the foot in late-March. Doctors at the time told Pierce to expect a four-to-six-month rehab process and Pierce returned to practice Aug. 27, just longer than two weeks before the team’s first game. He played a reduced number of snaps in Week 1 – 32 of 54 – but was set to play near a normal role in a Sunday Night Football contest in Week 2 in Kansas City before going down a quarter into the contest while running a route.

The fifth-year receiver was carted back to the locker room for imaging, and he was seen using crutches to exit the building following the team’s overtime loss. The Colts then placed Pierce on injured reserve, meaning he would miss at least the team’s next four games but be eligible to return as soon as Week 7 in Minnesota. Just days before that opportunity, Pierce was seen by reporters in the press box at the team’s Week 6 game at Lucas Oil Stadium in a walking boot.

“He’s still in the rehab process, and I’m not going to put a timetable on his return,” Steichen said Wednesday when asked whether it was still realistic for Pierce to return before the end of the season.

Currently on a five-game losing streak, the Colts sit 2-7 heading into a winnable Week 10 home matchup against the Dolphins, and Indianapolis is staring at one of the NFL’s easiest schedules over the rest of the season – only three of its final eight games are against teams in the playoff picture.

Tuesday, the Colts dealr the team’s top two healthy receivers in Josh Downs (to Kansas City) and Keenan Allen (to San Francisco). On Sunday, the team is slated to roll out Anthony Gould, Laquon Treadwell, Ashton Dulin, Deion Burks and Nick Westbrook-Ikhine as its options at receiver with Pierce still on IR – a group that has combined for 27 catches for 375 receiving yards this season.

Though Pierce has only played five quarters and 49 total offensive snaps this year, he still ranks top 3 on the team among rostered wideouts in catches (five) and receiving yards (72).

The Colts did open the 21-day practice window Wednesday for veteran edge rusher Arden Key, who has missed the Colts' last five games with a hamstring injury he suffered during the team’s Week 4 game in London. Key logged his first practice since suffering the injury on Wednesday and was a full participant.

text:
The dust has finally settled after a wild few weeks leading up to the trade deadline, with lots of big names in new places.

Unfortunately, lots of big names will be nowhere to be found -- at least not on the field -- as we enter Week 10. There were several injuries to key players in Week 9, none bigger than Puka Nacua suffering a significant knee injury. Though the Rams have not officially put the superstar wide receiver on IR, he is facing a multi-week absence as the Rams' snakebitten season continues. Other notable names going down with injury Sunday included Rhamondre Stevenson, Josh Jacobs, Malik Willis, Jaylen Waddle, Luther Burden III, Riley Moss and Antoine Winfield Jr.

Quarterbacks Patrick Mahomes (elbow) and Justin Herbert (finger/hand) appear to have avoided major injury, but their respective statuses are worth monitoring going forward, too. Herbert will have one extra day to heal as the Chargers play on Monday night against the Ravens.

Here's the initial injury report for each team playing on Sunday in Week 10, as well as the final injury report for the Giants-Commanders "Thursday Night Football" matchup.

Odds courtesy of DraftKings Sportsbook

Commanders at Giants (-2.5)

Commanders: C Lucas Patrick (concussion), TE Colson Yankoff (knee) OUT

Giants: LB Malik Harrison (groin) QUESTIONABLE

Washington will be down one starter in Patrick; Nick Allegretti figures to slot in there. Otherwise, it's a mostly clean injury report, with the return of Treylon Burks a potential boost for the downfield passing game. He missed Week 9 with a foot injury.

The Giants have one of their cleanest injury reports of the year. Notably, running back Cam Skattebo (hamstring) will be back after missing Week 9 with a hamstring injury, and coach John Harbaugh said he will be "full go" in this NFC East meeting.

Patriots at Lions (-2.5) in Munich

New England ruled out offensive lineman Ben Brown (knee), cornerback Carlton Davis III (knee) and running back TreVeyon Henderson (illness), and all three did not participate in Wednesday's practice. Also not participating were tight end Cameron Latu (back), offensive lineman Walter Rouse (concussion), safety Brenden Schooler (hamstring) and running back Rhamondre Stevenson (knee). Stevenson is expected to miss at least this week with the injury he suffered Sunday. Wide receiver A.J. Brown (ankle/knee), safety Kevin Byard III (chest), fullback Reggie Gilliam (knee), tight end Hunter Henry (foot), tackle Morgan Moses (foot), offensive lineman Greg Van Roten (hamstring) and cornerback Charles Woods (hamstring) were all limited. Brown hasn't played since Week 7 and has played in just three contests this year.

Center Cade Mays (ankle), cornerback D.J. Reed (hip) and running back Sione Vaki (ankle) did not practice Wednesday; Mays and Reed are considered long shots to play. Defensive back Brian Branch (hip), quarterback Jared Goff (chest), safety Kerby Joseph (knee) and wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown (rib) were all limited.

Texans (-4.5) at Browns

Four Texans players did not practice Wednesday: linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair (groin/personal), tight end Brevin Jordan (finger/foot), running back David Montgomery (groin) and offensive lineman Keylan Rutledge (neck/shoulder). Montgomery has not played since suffering the injury in Week 5. Wide receiver Tank Dell (hand/shoulder), running back Woody Marks (knee), safety Reed Blankenship (concussion/hand), wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. (hamstring), cornerback Jaylin Smith (hamstring), linebacker Jake Hummel (groin) and offensive lineman Wyatt Teller (illness) were all limited for Houston in ahead of a crucial matchup in the AFC playoff race.

Wide receiver Denzel Boston (toe), fullback Michael Burton (calf), safety Ronnie Hickman (concussion) and center Elgton Jenkins (knee) all did not practice for the Browns on Wednesday. Boston has played through a couple of injuries this year, and Jenkins has played through his knee ailment, too. Tackle Austin Barber (calf), defensive tackle Maliek Collins (elbow), tight end Harold Fannin Jr. (groin), tackle Tytus Howard (knee), linebacker Carson Schwesinger (wrist/ankle), cornerback Denzel Ward (cornerback) and linebacker Quincy Williams (hamstring) were all limited. Deshaun Watson, who cleared concussion protocol last week but did not play, was not on the injury report and will start this weekend. Shedeur Sanders played all of Cleveland's Week 9 loss to the Saints.

Chiefs (-3.5) at Falcons

The Chiefs listed two players as "DNP" on Wednesday: offensive lineman Jaylon Moore (ankle) and defensive lineman Peter Woods (neck), but by far the biggest news was Patrick Mahomes (elbow) being able to practice fully. He suffered what looked like a potentially serious elbow injury against the Jets but was able to return to the game. Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott (knee) was limited.

The Falcons were without wide receiver Zachariah Branch (hamstring), linebacker Josh Woods (ankle) and EDGE James Pearce Jr. (back). Branch missed last week's contest while Pearce, in his first game back from suspension, logged just 15 snaps after the back issue flared up late in the week. Defensive lineman Gervon Dexter St. (illness) and EDGE Za'Darius Smith (rest) also did not practice Wednesday. Linebacker Divine Deablo (forearm) was limited. He played with his arm wrapped in Week 9.

Panthers at Saints (-2.5)

The Panthers got a host of players back to practice Wednesday, which was really a walkthrough: EDGE Jaelan Phillips (hamstring), guard Damien Lewis (knee) and cornerback Will Lee III (hamstring) were all full participants. Phillips has missed the last three games, Lewis the last two and Lee the most recent one. Furthermore, cornerback Mike Jackson (groin), running back Jonathan Brooks (groin and wide receiver Xavier Legette (knee) were full participants after having their 21-day practice windows opened coming off IR. Linebacker Bobby Okereke (foot) and running back Chuba Hubbard (rest) did not participate.

The biggest returnee -- at least to practice -- for the Saints is running back Travis Etienne Jr., who remains on IR. He was limited with a hamstring injury. Running backs CJ Donaldson (shoulder). Alvin Kamara (rest/back) and center Erik McCoy (biceps) did not practice, and coach Kellen Moore said Cesar Ruiz will start at center this week. Tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. (ankle), guard David Edwards (knee), cornerback Martin Emerson Jr. (shin), tight end Noah Fant (back) and defensive lineman Christen Miller (knee) joined Etienne in the "limited" category.

Vikings at Packers (-3)

After playing on "Monday Night Football," the Vikings did not practice Wednesday, so their injury report reflects an estimate of participation. Linebacker Blake Cashman (concussion), tight end T.J. Hockenson (wrist/chest), defensive lineman Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins (ankle), wide receiver Jauan Jennings (calf), quarterback Kyler Murray (hamstring) and EDGE Kyle Van Noy (calf) were all listed as non-participants, while quarterback Carson Wentz (ankle) and safety Jay Ward (knee) were listed as limited. Coach Kevin O'Connell was hopeful Wentz would be able to back up newly acquired Kirk Cousins against Green Bay.

The Packers, meanwhile, reported that safety Javon Bullard (ankle/knee), linebacker Zaire Franklin (shin), offensive lineman Sean Rhyan (ankle), EDGE Lukas Van Ness (back) and tight end Josh Whyle (concussion) did not participate. Green Bay only held a jog-through, so the reports are an estimate. Guard Aaron Banks (knee/hip), running back Chris Brooks (ankle), offensive lineman Travis Glover (knee), linebacker Ty'Ron Hopper (illness), wide receiver Skyy Moore (ankle), EDGE Micah Parsons (knee/illness), kicker Trey Smack (calf), wide receiver Savion Williams (groin) and guard Kevin Zeitler (ankle) did not participate. Parsons remains on the PUP list, while Moore and Brooks are in their 21-day practice window.

Bills (-8.5) at Jets

The Bills, who played Monday night, only conducted a walk-through on Wednesday. Offensive lineman Alec Anderson (ankle), cornerback Christian Benford (wrist), tackle Spencer Brown (ankle), tackle Dion Dawkins (rib), tight end Dalton Kincaid (ankle) and center Connor McGovern (neck) were all limited. Anderson and Dawkins both missed Monday's win over the Vikings.

In their estimation, the Jets listed defensive lineman Harrison Phillips (ankle) and linebacker Trevin Wallace (groin) as "did not practice" Wednesday. Wide receivers Omar Cooper Jr. (ankle) and Garrett Wilson (concussion), EDGE Joseph Ossai (ankle), cornerback Nahshon Wright (back) and safety VJ Payne (knee) were all estimated to be limited. Wilson, the team's top wide receiver, did not play last week.

Jaguars (-10.5) at Titans

The Jaguars' big trade deadline additions -- safety Jessie Bates III and defensive tackle Jordan Davis -- did not participate Wednesday, with "rest" listed as the reason for both. Also not practicing were wide receiver Jakobi Meyers (ankle), running back Bhayshul Tuten (ankle/foot) and defensive end Travon Walker (rib). Meyers, Tuten and Walker all played through said injuries last week. Offensive linemen Ezra Cleveland (knee/ankle) and Robert Hainsey (concussion), safety Antonio Johnson (ankle), running back Chris Rodriguez Jr. (hand) and linebacker Brason Combs (shoulder) were limited.

The Titans had five players -- linebackers Cody Barton (concussion) and Anthony Hill Jr. (neck), guard Peter Skoronski (hamstring), running back Tyjae Spears (knee) and wide receiver Carnell Tate (shoulder) listed as not participating. Tate and Spears both missed the Titans' last game, back in Week 8 before the team's bye, too.

Dolphins at Colts (-3.5)

Center Aaron Brewer (concussion) and tight end Will Kacmarek (quad/knee) were the only two Dolphins players not participating Wednesday. Long snapper Tucker Addington (shoulder), cornerback Darrell Baker Jr. (knee), wide receiver Chris Bell (knee) and EDGE Malik Herring (neck) were all limited. The team placed quarterback Malik Willis and defensive tackle Zach Sieler on IR on Tuesday, with Sieler's injury season-ending.

The Colts said tight end Mo Alie-Cox (groin), linebacker Jaylon Carlies (neck), linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither (knee), safety AJ Haulcy (ankle), long snapper Luke Rhodes (hamstring), tackle Jalen Travis and cornerback Charvarius Ward (rest) did not practice. Running back Jonathan Taylor (rest) and defensive tackle Jerry Tillery (calf) were limited.

Rams (-9.5) at Cardinals

The Rams were without wide receiver Puka Nacua (knee/toe), cornerback Trent McDuffie (back), tight end Terrance Ferguson (ankle/hamstring), offensive lineman Steve Avila (hamstring) and safety Kam Curl (toe) at practice Wednesday. as has been the case all year, the star-studded group is quite banged up, though Sean McVay was optimistic McDuffie would return after missing Week 9. Tight end Davis Allen (oblique), long snapper Joe Cardona (ankle), defensive lineman Myles Garrett (knee) and tight end Colby Parkinson (ribs) were limited.

For the Cardinals, safety Budda Baker (rest), center Hjalte Froholdt (concussion), guard Jon Gaines II (ankle), defensive lineman Roy Loyez (toe/ankle), offensive lineman Isaac Seumalo (rest), EDGE Josh Sweat (rest) and linebacker Mack Wilson Sr. (rest/knee/ankle) did not participate. Running back Bam Knight (concussion), tight end Hunter Long (knee), cornerback Max Melton (knee/hand), defensive linemen Dante Stills (shoulder) and Zach Carter (knee), tackle Jayden Williams (knee) and safety Andrew Wingard (groin) were limited.

Seahawks (-6.5) at Raiders

The Seahawks released a lengthy Wednesday injury report that featured seven "DNP" designations. The biggest one is that Sam Darnold (ribs, quad) remains out, and the team will start Drew Lock (elbow, oblique) in Week 10, even though he was listed as limited. Joining Darnold in not participating were tackle Charles Cross (ankle), guard Quenton Nelson (knee), defensive tackles Brandon Pili (back) and Jarran Reed (personal), wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba (rest) and defensive end Leonard Williams (stinger). Along with Lock, guard Anthony Bradford (knee), EDGE Derick Hall (back), EDGE Uchenna Nwosu (ankle), linebacker Patrick O'Connell (toe) and EDGE Connor O'Toole (foot) were limited.

Every active Raiders player participated at least somewhat in the team's Wednesday practice. Defensive tackles Thomas Booker (ankle) and Foley Fotukasi (shoulder/back) were limited, as was guard Trey Zuhn III (concussion).

49ers (-4.5) at Cowboys

Wide receiver Mike Evans (Achilles), cornerback Renardo Greene (back), linebacker Dre Greenlaw (rest), cornerback Deommodore Lenoir (foot), running back Christian McCaffrey (rest) and tackle Trent Williams (rest) did not participate in 49ers practice Wednesday. Safety Siran Neal (knee, foot), cornerback Upton Stout (shoulder, neck), wide receiver Deebo Samuel (hamstring) and defensive tackle C.J. West (knee) were all limited. West had his practice window opened.

For the Cowboys, EDGE Donovan Ezeiruaku (ankle), tight end Jake Ferguson (knee/ankle), running back Tyler Goodson (ankle/knee), safety Malik Hooker (personal), defensive back P.J. Locke (concussion), EDGE Von Miller (rest), wide receiver Jonathan Mingo (ankle) and cornerback Joey Porter Jr. (ankle) did not practice. Ferguson and Goodson will miss extended periods, and Porter missed last week. Linebacker DeMarvion Overshown (hamstring/back), wide receiver George Pickens (hamstring) and wide receiver KaVontae Turpin (ribs) were limited. Overshown and Pickens missed last week, and Turpin has not played since mid-October.

Steelers at Bengals (-3.5)

Tight end Darnell Washington (rest), EDGE T.J. Watt (rest) and defensive tackle Cameron Heyward (rest) were the only Steelers who did not participate Wednesday. Safety DeShon Elliott (ankle) and defensive tackle Derrick Harmon (foot) were both limited; Harmon is currently designated to return from injured reserve and has not played since Week 4.

text:
ALLEN PARK — The Detroit Lions are expecting to get at least one player back for their game against the New England Patriots at Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany, on Sunday, Nov. 15.

Lions coach Dan Campbell said Wednesday, Nov. 11, that DJ Wonnum (concussion) has cleared the first two obstacles necessary to return to practice and "should be good to go" against New England "as long as he gets through practice."

Wonnum suffered his injury against the Minnesota Vikings on Nov. 1 when he had a head-to-head collision with safety Brian Branch during a tackle of receiver Justin Jefferson. He missed last week's game against the Miami Dolphins.

As for cornerback D.J. Reed (hip) and center Cade Mays (ankle), Campbell said both players have a "way, way, way outside shot" of playing against New England and likely won't practice on Wednesday.

Reed and Mays were both injured in the Vikings game as well. Reed suffered a hip injury on a pass breakup in the fourth quarter and Mays suffered an ankle injury in the second quarter.

The good news for Detroit is that it has gotten solid play from its backup center. Juice Scruggs filled in admirably as Mays missed the season's first five games with a wrist injury and stepped right back in for a 19-9 win over the Dolphins.

With Reed out of the lineup, the Lions will continue relying on a rotation of Rock Ya-Sin, Roger McCreary, Ennis Rakestraw and Khalil Dorsey.

text:
The Steelers began their preparation for Sunday night's game against the Cincinnati Bengals, a key AFC North matchup with first place in the division on the line once again.

With the Steelers coming off the bye week, it was an opportunity for several players to get healthy, with multiple players eligible to return to practice this week.

Defensive tackle Derrick Harmon returned to practice today but remains on the Reserve/Injured List.

The Steelers have a 21-day window to either activate Harmon or he remains on the Reserve/Injured List for the remainder of the season. He was placed on the Reserve/Injured List on October 10.

Harmon, the Steelers No. 1 pick in the 2025 NFL Draft, appeared in four games this year, with one start, before he was placed on the Reserve/Injured List. He has 12 tackles this season, including three solo stops and a tackle for a loss. He also has one and a half sacks and a forced fumble.

In two seasons, Harmon has appeared in 16 games, with nine starts. He is credited with 39 tackles, including 14 solo tackles, as well as two tackles for a loss. He also has four and a half sacks, a pass defense and a forced fumble.

Receiver Michael Pittman Jr. is also eligible to return but hasn't yet. Pittman said last week he would like to return 'sooner rather than later' and McCarthy sees the progress he is making.

"I think Michael is getting close," said McCarthy on Monday. "I know his workout, I'm going to say Friday, was something that hopefully we can do more.

"We just want to get our guys, get them healthy. We're going to be obviously healthier than we've been in a while. So, it will be good to see really what Wednesday gives us as far as who we think is going to be ready for Cincinnati."

In addition, receiver Roman Wilson is eligible to come off the Reserve/Injured List following the Bengals game. Whether he returns to practice immediately is yet to be seen, but having everyone available would be a benefit to the offense.

"I think it will help all of them for sure," said offensive coordinator Brian Angelichio. "I think any time you can get your full group of guys back, it certainly eliminates the stress that other guys have to do to pick up the load."

With the situation the Steelers have dealt with at receiver over the last month with injuries, rookie Germie Bernard has become a go-to guy for quarterback Aaron Rodgers.

Bernard, who has started four games, has 32 receptions for 284 yards, an 8.9-yard average, and one touchdown.

"He's just getting more comfortable," said offensive coordinator Brian Angelichio. "You see the trust growing between them. He's really good with the ball in his hands, the run after the catch. It's a great job by Aaron getting him the ball, and he got us down to the one-yard line (against Cleveland), and then we clocked it.

"That was a great check, and guys are blocking downfield for him, (Pat Freiermuth) and DK (Metcalf), and Germ made it come to life. I think that's his strength. You saw it on the bubble early in the game in the run solution. He's always going forward. He's a tough tackle. He's got good explosion.

"I think the more he plays, the more trust, I think the more you'll see of it."

While the secondary is trending toward being a healthy group again, two players who have handled the next man up mentality through the first half of the season have been rookies Daylen Everett and Robert Spears-Jennings.

"They work really hard, and we hold them to a certain standard in terms of it doesn't matter, it's next man up when they get in the game, and those guys work really hard," said defensive coordinator Patrick Graham. "I enjoy seeing them play football. They're good football players.

"Both are physical. Both have a knack for getting to the ball. Then they work really hard, and they don't have a lot of repeat mistakes. I can't speak for the vets, but that's how they're earning the trust of the vets. Not a lot of repeat mistakes, they work hard, and they're a joy to be around."

text:
HOUSTON - Houston Texans QB C.J. Stroud has been named AFC Offensive Player of the Week, the NFL announced today.

In Week 9, Stroud earned a 125.5 passer rating while completing 21-of-35 (60.0%) passes for 384 yards and five touchdowns in a 44-22 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers. The Texans opened the game on an eight-play, 73-yard drive, where Stroud completed five-of-five passes for 53 yards and a touchdown.

Stroud's five passing touchdowns tied his career high and marked the second time in his career that he has thrown for 350 yards while passing for five touchdowns, and his first since Nov. 5, 2023, versus Tampa Bay. His 384 passing yards and five touchdowns led the NFL in both categories in Week 9, and he recorded the third highest passer rating (125.5) in the NFL in Week 9. Stroud helped lead the Texans offense to the highest point total in the AFC in Week 9 (44), while being the only AFC quarterback to throw for over 300 passing yards. The Texans 44 points was tied for the most in franchise in a road game.

On the year, Stroud has completed 181-of-282 (64.2%) passes for 2,251 yards, 16 touchdowns and a passer rating of 104.8. Stroud leads the AFC in touchdown to interception ratio (8.0), is tied for first in completions of at least 20 yards (32), ranks second in passing yards per game (281.4) and ranks third in passer rating.

This marks the former Offensive Rookie of the Year's fifth AFC Offensive Player of the Week honor of his career. Stroud is the first player to win the AFC Offensive Player of the Week Award multiple times this season, and the first to do so since Josh Allen in 2025 (Week 1, Week 11 and Week 14).

title: Cardinals to start rookie QB Carson Beck against Rams - ESPN
authors: Josh Weinfuss, Stephen Holder, Ben Solak, Kevin Seifert, Nate Taylor, Liz Loza, Tristan H. Cockcroft, NFL Nation, Michael DiRocco, ESPN staff
description:
TEMPE, Ariz. -- Arizona Cardinals rookie quarterback Carson Beck will make his NFL debut Sunday against the Los Angeles Rams, coach Mike LaFleur said Wednesday.
Beck, a third-round pick by Arizona, spent the first eight weeks as the Cardinals' emergency third quarterback and was inactive on game day.
"It's really been a welcome to the NFL season that just getting introduced to what the league is and what it can be."
As the backup, Beck doubled his workload running the scout team offense, according to quarterbacks coach Matt Schaub.
LaFleur said playing in his first NFL game with receivers he knows well will be beneficial to Beck.
text:
TEMPE, Ariz. -- Arizona Cardinals rookie quarterback Carson Beck will make his NFL debut Sunday against the Los Angeles Rams, coach Mike LaFleur said Wednesday.

Quarterback Gardner Minshew II was placed on injured reserve Tuesday after suffering a UCL injury in his throwing arm Sunday at Seattle, paving the way for Beck to get his first career start.

Beck, a third-round pick by Arizona, spent the first eight weeks as the Cardinals' emergency third quarterback and was inactive on game day. He was the backup against the Seahawks after Arizona traded Jacoby Brissett to Baltimore.

"Obviously having gone from emergency quarterback at the beginning of the season to last week being the backup to now being the starter, I mean, it's been a crazy season," Beck said. "It's really been a welcome to the NFL season that just getting introduced to what the league is and what it can be."

LaFleur said Beck, who played in 55 games over six seasons at Georgia and Miami, won't be fazed by the moment.

"I know this isn't too big for him," LaFleur said. "Go have some fun, man. Go let it sling."

Beck's last start came in January in the CFP National Championship game, which Miami lost to Indiana 27-21. The game before, Beck led the Hurricanes to a win over Ole Miss in the CFP quarterfinals at the Fiesta Bowl at State Farm Stadium, where he'll play Sunday.

"Obviously that was a super cool moment for me, probably my favorite game I've ever played in," Beck said. "So there's some good moments I've already had in that stadium, but it'll be really cool to walk in that stadium and know what's at stake and what's to come on Sunday for sure."

LaFleur said he wants to see Beck continue what he has been doing in practice and treat each play individually.

"You never really know until you get to the live bullets on Sunday, but just the way he goes about his business ... have all the confidence that he's ready to roll," the coach said.

LaFleur said Beck "will not be scared" of letting it fly in his NFL debut. As the backup, Beck doubled his workload running the scout team offense, according to quarterbacks coach Matt Schaub.

"He can translate those into getting himself prepared, moving around the pocket, not just going through the motions, and he's really diligent on that and just going through his process, which he's been doing all year, but it's just those physical reps," Schaub said.

Schaub said he saw a change in Beck's demeanor with the increased reps.

"He's a confident kid by nature, so he's reserved, but I mean he's been what he's been since he's been here," Schaub said. "And so it's been good to see him getting his workload ramped up, especially he had some little injury situation in camp, so he lost some reps and some experience and just development there, but he's picked back up and so we like where he's at."

Beck was asked about his growth this season and mentioned the difference in the playbook: "You go all the way back to when I first got here and rookie minicamp, OTAs, I mean, just trying to say a whole playcall in the huddle is not the easiest thing ever. I did a little bit at Georgia. We had pretty long playcalls. Miami, a little bit shorter, but we had a couple long ones.

"But again, just in that standpoint of things, looking at it, being able to operate and get in and out of the huddle, communicate well, I think that's a huge thing that obviously I've got a ton of practice at. So it's something that I've definitely got better at."

LaFleur credited Beck's college experience for helping him prepare to start.

"He's been a pro since he's been here," LaFleur said. "He puts in the exact amount of work that he needs. And then from a physical standpoint, he'll obviously get 100% of the reps."

Beck said sitting for three years at Georgia "prepared me for this -- of how to handle yourself like a pro when you are on the sideline, when you are the backup, how to still prepare like you are the starter. You have to learn those things.

"That's a skill that you have to, through trial and error, figuring out what kind of schedule do I want to have for myself so that when you do get your opportunity, you're not doing anything new, you're just doing the same stuff and now you're obviously just going out there and actually the guy doing it."

Beck will be throwing to a number of familiar receivers he worked with on the practice squad before he was the No. 2 quarterback last week. Arizona's currently active receiving corps of Simi Fehoko, Reggie Virgil and Devin Duvernay has a combined eight catches this season. However, Beck's tight end corps of Trey McBride, Elijah Higgins and Teagan Quitoriano has 94 combined.

LaFleur said playing in his first NFL game with receivers he knows well will be beneficial to Beck.

"He knows how these guys move and he knows the indicators that they're given," LaFleur said. "So, he sees them in the huddle, albeit with no one watching. I mean it's going to be a little bit different on Sunday, but absolutely."

LaFleur made it official Wednesday that Minshew needs surgery and will miss the rest of the season. With their quarterback room depleted, the Cardinals added veteran Josh Johnson and Joey Aguilar to the active roster Tuesday. LaFleur worked with Johnson in 2020 with the 49ers, and in 2021 with the Jets.

LaFleur said Arizona was interested in Aguilar during the draft process, but after selecting Beck and with a stocked quarterback room of veterans, the Cardinals didn't have room for another signal-caller.

"So, it just ran its course at that point, had some interest in him," LaFleur said. "When all this unfolded, it was an easy deal for us."

Jonathan Taylor, Daniel Jones and Brian Thomas Jr. were arguably the buzziest names before the deadline but didn't move. Why not?

Graziano: In Taylor's case, it's because the "buzz" never lined up with the Colts' desire to trade him. Remember, Quenton Nelson, DeForest Buckner and Keenan Allen were all in the final year of their contracts. Taylor is not. He's 27 years old and signed for two more years. They didn't have to trade him. He can be part of the solution next year and beyond. So they held firm on their price, asking for a first-round pick or some package of picks that would be reasonably equivalent to that. And no team emerged that was willing to give them that.

The important thing to remember about Taylor is that the Colts never had an interest in moving on from him to just clear salary or be rid of the player. They like him. He's the only one of their prominent veterans who were extension-eligible last summer and actually got an extension. (Alec Pierce and Jones were free agents, remember.) So while there were talks, I don't get the sense the Colts were ever eager or close to trading Taylor.

Fowler: The buzz around Taylor persisted because of interest from other teams, the franchise's teardown tone set by the Nelson/Buckner trades and the sheer mileage on the player (1,712 carries). But he's a boon for any Indy coaching staff in 2027. He's also the team's best player. While Josh Downs clearly wanted out, Taylor wasn't as dug in (though I'm sure he would have welcomed the chance to play for a contender). My sense in talking to teams is that Indy wanted at least a first-round equivalent in any package, and interested teams couldn't get there. I believe Denver gave it a run this week but wasn't comfortable with the return Indianapolis was seeking.

As for Jones, he was likely Minnesota's backup option to Cousins. It's worth noting that the Colts' coaching staff just doesn't seem eager to play Anthony Richardson Sr. and is much more comfortable with Jones despite his struggles. So I believe that's a factor in all of this.

Graziano: Jones, who turns 30 next May, will be a decision for the incoming GM and (possibly) next head coach to make in the offseason. He's scheduled to earn $38 million in 2027. None of that is guaranteed at the moment -- $10.51 million of it becomes fully guaranteed if he's still on the roster on the fifth day of the 2027 league year. If Jones finishes the season playing well, and the team can legitimately talk itself into the idea that he'll be better next year further removed from his Achilles injury, that price could make him an attractive option. If not, Indianapolis can cut him without too much pain. It would take on $35.2 million in dead money cap charges in 2027, but that's not as intimidating a number as it used to be.

Fowler: Thomas, meanwhile, garnered significant interest, but in the end the Jaguars, a true contender, didn't want to subtract. They only wanted to add. And they value Thomas, though his numbers don't reflect that. He has speed that demands defensive attention.

Graziano: Thomas doesn't appear to be an important player for the Jaguars anymore when you check the box score, but look around the league. The Rams are almost out of receivers. The 49ers have been scrambling to fill those spots all season. Injuries happen, and if something should happen to Jakobi Meyers or Parker Washington, the Jaguars believe Thomas could help them if he suddenly got thrust into a higher-volume role. The Jaguars are very clearly thinking about getting the top seed in the AFC and winning the Super Bowl. Maintaining quality depth at premium positions is important.

Fowler: What's tough about Thomas' situation is he has only one reception in the past four games, and my sense is the player would have welcomed a fresh start had a trade happened. But that's a lot of talent on which to give up. Thomas was, quite easily, the most gifted athlete on the field when I visited Jaguars training camp. So while Taylor staying in Indy was a matter of the Colts' high demands, I don't think that was the case with Thomas. The Jaguars could have gotten a quality pick for him. They just didn't seem interested in moving him, even though he could have helped recoup some of the lost capital from Monday's flurry of trades.

But Jacksonville should probably try to find a way to get Thomas involved more. It will need him in January.

What now for the Vikings and Raiders after Kirk Cousins was traded to Minnesota?

Fowler: Cousins is comfort food for Minnesota. He's predictable. And more importantly, he's predictable in Kevin O'Connell's offense. He removes at least some unknown variables that could derail a promising season. Kyler Murray hadn't proved to be a fit in this specific scheme (which could have been detected back in, say, March), and Carson Wentz was just bad. In fact, had Wentz simply played passable football Monday night, I'm not so sure Minnesota would have stretched draft capital to get quarterback help. Murray would have been back from injury eventually and perhaps Minnesota could have adjusted to his skill set.

But Monday night was dire, so it's time to salvage the season with a quarterback who knows the system and played well in Las Vegas. Cousins is essentially a half-season option with a chance to re-sign. His $10 million roster bonus in 2027 is guaranteed. He has a two-year, $80 million extension that kicks in on the fifth day of the new league year, effectively serving as a poison pill. The Vikings most likely won't pay that, but they can either pay him $10 million to walk away or repackage it in a new deal.

What the Vikings do at backup quarterback will be fascinating. Either Murray or Wentz can serve as QB2. There's also the option to release one or place one on injured reserve. (Murray already has an injury, and Wentz appeared to hurt his throwing hand Monday night.) Either way, QB1 is solidified, at least for a half-season. And Minnesota didn't have to give up a pick in the top two rounds to make it happen.

Graziano: I agree with you and honestly don't believe that the Vikings wanted to trade for a quarterback. They believed Murray would play better than he did in Week 8 in Detroit and obviously didn't know he'd get injured in that game. And Wentz played considerably worse Monday than anyone in the Vikings' building thought he would. So they spent the early hours of Tuesday morning examining the landscape and what was possible, looking at options that included Cousins, Daniel Jones and Geno Smith.

From what I have been told, the Raiders weren't looking to trade Cousins, who has played well for them and allowed them to hold off on playing Fernando Mendoza as long as possible. The Vikings had checked in on Cousins last week to get a sense of what it might cost if they decided to go down that road, but they didn't get the sense that Cousins was available prior to Sunday.

Minnesota was desperate enough in the wake of its recent offensive disappointments to offer a third-round pick, and the Raiders decided Mendoza was ready enough that they could afford to move on from Cousins. The Vikings had an extra third-round pick as a result of their trade of Jonathan Greenard to the Eagles. (They traded their original third-round pick in this deal, so they still have the Eagles' third-rounder, which at this point looks likely to be much higher.)

This is a deal that really came together Tuesday because it was deadline day. Had the deadline been two weeks from now, the Vikings might have decided to roll with their initial plan a while longer, especially if Murray is going to be healthy enough to play in the next week or so. But if they didn't do a deal Tuesday, they weren't going to have a chance to fix their problem for the rest of the season. Cousins is expected to step in right away as Minnesota's starter, and ideally he plays well enough to keep that job the rest of the year. Because the Vikings have already had their bye and the Raiders haven't had theirs, Cousins could end up playing in 18 games this season.

Fowler: This move helps Minnesota get through the season -- and keeps Justin Jefferson happy -- but does little to solve the team's long-term quarterback issues. The Vikings have badly mismanaged the QB room for a few years now. GM Nolan Teasley was hired May 30, and he inherited much of this mess. But the team's 2024 starter (Sam Darnold) is a Super Bowl winner in Seattle. The 2025 starter (J.J. McCarthy) was booted after 10 starts and is thriving in New York. The 2026 starter (Murray) is injured and essentially soft-benched. And the 2023 starter (Cousins) is the Week 10 starter in 2026.

That's not how you want to manage a roster at the game's most important position. And it raises serious questions about where the Vikings go next. Teasley, in his first full offseason with the team, will have a big impact on that process.

Graziano: Yeah, that's a grim-but-accurate rundown of the situation, and the Vikings are well aware of it. I think that's one of the reasons they weren't really excited about having to wade into the QB market again so soon and deal away a pick that could have theoretically assisted them in addressing the situation in a more meaningful way next offseason. This is a move for this season, by a team that won its first six games, has an incredible defense that's playing out of its mind and boasts two first-round picks at wide receiver.

The Vikings owed it to this season's roster to make sure they weren't caught short again at quarterback. They will be back on this hamster wheel next spring, but it was important to them that they stop it from spinning for the rest of this season at least. Cousins helps them do that in theory. He has 20 touchdown passes this season. The Vikings have scored a total of 13 touchdowns as a team, and five of those were in Week 1.

What is your best piece of fantasy football advice for this week?

Graziano: I would add Texans receiver Tank Dell if he's available on your league's waiver wire. Houston's receivers room suddenly feels crowded and unpredictable, but C.J. Stroud is playing his tail off, the Texans' offense seems to be hitting its stride, and Dell sure looked all the way back from injury, catching four passes for 105 yards and a touchdown in Sunday's beatdown of the hapless Chargers.

It'll be tougher sledding this week against the Browns, but Dell was targeted nine times Sunday; no other Texan was targeted more than five times. He can threaten deep and do some of the stuff they had planned for Jaylin Noel before Noel got hurt. We know that Dell and Stroud have a deep friendship and connection from the early part of their careers before Dell's injury. He could be a high-volume helper the rest of the way.

Fowler: Packers running back Kaleb Johnson seems worth the play this week. While Johnson is splitting carries with MarShawn Lloyd because of Josh Jacobs' injury, the Packers like the vision Johnson showed last week vs. New England in producing 68 yards and a touchdown on 14 carries. They could give Johnson an extended look this week vs. the Vikings. I'm not confident in Green Bay's rushing attack, but at least the offense could choose to ride the hot hand here.

What else are you hearing?

Graziano: The Steelers were in the market for wide receiver help, and I was told they were in discussions with Tennessee about Calvin Ridley. But while the Titans dealt away a couple of key defensive players in Amani Hooker and Jeffery Simmons, they stayed true to their word about holding the offense together to give Cam Ward a chance to continue his development.

Fowler: A Ridley deal for a late-round pick would have made sense, but the player's recent incident at the Nashville airport gave some teams pause in recent days. The Steelers were also interested in now-Chiefs receiver Josh Downs, but their lack of a fourth-round pick in 2027 complicated any pursuit. The Steelers wanted to preserve their draft capital within reason, in part because of their long-term quarterback uncertainty.

Consider: The teams that made aggressive trades in recent days have star quarterbacks in place. But if the Steelers need to acquire a passer in the future via the draft or free agency, that requires a reserve of capital. Plus, veterans Roman Wilson and Michael Pittman Jr. should return from injury soon.

Graziano: Edge rusher Josh Sweat and safety Budda Baker were a couple of names people around the league thought could get dealt at this deadline. Teams checked in on both, but nothing ever got to the point of a deal for either.

Fowler: The Cowboys did not receive any trade calls on receiver George Pickens, who is happy in Dallas and didn't want to be traded. Teams in the receiver market weren't shopping in the high-end aisle, either, so the idea of a Pickens trade was a nonstarter. Plus, Dallas had no plans to deal him.

Graziano: With all the defensive tackles moving around, teams called the Panthers about Derrick Brown -- but were told no.

Fowler: The Browns looked for an extra edge rusher and a blocking tight end and put out several feelers, but nothing came together. This was the rare cycle in which Cleveland did not make a move.

Graziano: People around the league thought what the Jaguars gave up in the Jordan Davis deal was too high, but it's worth noting that Jacksonville had a few more hurdles in this year's defensive tackle market than other teams did. The Jaguars had interest in Jeffery Simmons and DeForest Buckner, but they played for teams in Jacksonville's division, so they were understandably either off-limits or far more costly for the Jags than they were for the Bears and 49ers.

Fowler: Part of the reason the Jaguars were comfortable giving up those premium picks is because they plan to work the compensatory pick formula and hopefully hit on their middle-round picks. For example, the Jaguars gave up second- and fifth-round picks for Jessie Bates III, but should Bates walk in free agency, he would most likely net a third- or fourth-round comp pick. General manager James Gladstone came from the Rams, who offset trading away first-round picks by shrewd evaluation in the middle to late rounds. Jacksonville will employ a similar strategy.

Graziano: Buffalo was scouring the league for help on the back end of its defense. Baker was among the names on the Bills' list. But they ended up with Hooker, who somewhat hilariously gets to play against the Jets for the second -- but not final -- time this season in his first game with the Bills on Sunday. Hooker and the Titans lost to the Jets in Week 1, but Buffalo hasn't played either of its games against the Jets yet this season, so Hooker will get two chances to avenge that loss.

Fowler: The Bills were clearly the most aggressive team on a somewhat slow deadline day. Word surfaced early Tuesday that Buffalo was clearing cap space via contract restructuring. Teams believed Buffalo was seeking impactful safeties and/or defensive tackles. The Bills made a play for Baker with what one source considered a compelling package. Arizona did not want to trade him because he's viewed as the heart and soul of the team. But the Bills were also working on Hooker, and it took a counteroffer of sorts to make that deal happen. The Titans originally resisted an offer for Hooker, whom they planned to keep; coach Robert Saleh loves him on the roster. But Buffalo tried again, pushing it to the finish line. It has been a busy few days all around for Bills GM Brandon Beane.

Fowler: The Chargers said no to at least one Ladd McConkey inquiry. Teams I spoke to believe the Rams were the ones to make that call. Overall, though, the Rams didn't seriously consider a receiver move because they expect both Puka Nacua and Davante Adams to return this season. And in the short term, they believe Matthew Stafford can maximize the supporting cast of receivers.

Graziano: The Rams certainly could have used help at receiver, where Adams and Jordan Whittington are on IR, and Nacua might be headed there as well. But remember, because of the Myles Garrett and Trent McDuffie trades, the Rams are extremely short on future draft capital relative to the other teams that were looking to add. The Rams have only four picks in next year's draft. They're without their first-, third- and seventh-round picks in 2027. They're also without their second-round pick in 2028 and their third-round pick in 2029 because of the Garrett trade. Frankly, they made their big moves in the offseason and were always going to have a tough time doing one at the deadline.

I found it interesting that the Rams placed Whittington on injured reserve Tuesday but did not do the same with Nacua. Rams coach Sean McVay said Monday that Nacua was likely to land on injured reserve because of knee and toe injuries, but so far he has not. If the Rams put him on IR, the soonest he could return is Week 15 against the Cowboys.

Being on IR means you must miss at least four games, not weeks, and the Rams have a bye in Week 11. So if they think it's possible Nacua might only have to miss four weeks, they could refrain from putting him on IR and possibly have him back in time for their Week 14 game at San Francisco. This all becomes moot if they put Nacua on IR this week, but just keep an eye on the situation if they don't. Speaking to people close to this situation Monday evening, they were very adamant that Nacua's injury isn't season-ending and that they hope to get him back for Week 14 or 15.

Nacua was targeted 19 times Sunday in a game in which Stafford threw 43 passes. He caught 14 of those passes for 150 yards and a touchdown. To say he'll be missed is an understatement. One note to keep in mind, though: The Rams went through their entire week of game prep planning to have a fully healthy tight end Terrance Ferguson against Washington. He was a big part of their game plan, and they left the practice field Friday -- less than 48 hours before kickoff -- feeling good about it. Then they found out that Ferguson had pulled a hamstring in Friday's practice and had to miss the game.

So, "just throw it to Puka" was a pretty good recovery plan given how little time they had to revise everything. I would expect the Rams to have a very different plan this week in Arizona. They were very happy with the way Blake Corum was running the ball Sunday and would feel pretty good about having to lean on the running game in the short term, particularly if Garrett is going to have the effect on the defense he had Sunday.

Fowler: The 49ers looked around for tight end help, and the Broncos' Evan Engram was on their radar. But they landed on Keenan Allen, who's a bigger receiver and perhaps serves some of the same functions in the offense.

Fowler: The Broncos received some interest in running back J.K. Dobbins. Had they moved on Jonathan Taylor, perhaps they would have entertained trading Dobbins. But Denver has two running backs on IR, so it needs both Jonah Coleman and Dobbins right now.

Fowler: Right tackle Braden Smith was a trade candidate in recent days. He's out of the rotation in Houston. A handful of teams showed interest in a potential deal, but nothing materialized.

Fowler: The Commanders received multiple calls on corner Mike Sainristil, a 2024 second-rounder who's out of the rotation in the Washington secondary. The Commanders were parting with Sainristil only for a quality pick, though.

Fowler: Seattle defensive tackle Jarran Reed was a trade candidate. Several teams had him on their lists. But Seattle was not motivated to move him. And the Bucs had strong interest in veteran defensive lineman A'Shawn Robinson, but they rarely trade at the deadline and are still in the NFC South race.

text:
NFL Week 10 brings another round of significant injury concerns across the league, with several key players facing uncertain availability and others already expected to miss time.

SICscore.com is tracking the latest NFL Week 10 injury news, practice participation, game-day designations and potential return timelines. This report will be updated throughout the week as teams release new information and final injury reports.

Wednesday, November 11th

DNP

Kyler Murray, Vikings - Hamstring

Murray is projected as a nonparticipant on Wednesday's injury report as he continues recovering from a hamstring injury. Vikings head coach Kevin O'Connell said Murray began his running progression Wednesday, marking a step in his rehabilitation. Minnesota did not hold practice, so the injury designation is an estimate.

Mike Evans, 49ers - Achilles

Evans will not practice Wednesday as he continues recovering from an Achilles injury that has sidelined him since before San Francisco's Week 8 bye. The 49ers wide receiver remains week-to-week, according to head coach Kyle Shanahan.

David Montgomery, Texans - Groin

Montgomery did not practice Wednesday as he continues recovering from a groin injury that sidelined him for Sunday's Week 9 game against the Chargers. The Texans running back is at risk of missing another game in Week 10, with Woody Marks handling the bulk of the backfield work in his absence.

Tyjae Spears, Titans - Knee

Spears did not practice Wednesday as he continues dealing with a lingering knee injury that has sidelined him since Week 7. The Titans running back missed Weeks 7 and 8, and the team's recent bye week has not provided enough recovery time for him to resume practicing ahead of Week 10.

LIMITED

George Pickens, Cowboys - Hamstring

Pickens was limited in Wednesday's practice as he continues recovering from a hamstring injury that sidelined him for Sunday's Week 9 game against the Colts. The Cowboys wide receiver was limited throughout last week's practices before ultimately being held out. His return to practice is an encouraging sign ahead of Sunday's Week 10 matchup against the 49ers.

Deebo Samuel, 49ers - Hamstring

Samuel is expected to be limited in Wednesday's practice as he continues recovering from a hamstring injury that has sidelined him since October 11. The 49ers wide receiver missed Sunday's Week 9 victory over the Raiders and is working toward a return in Week 10.

FULL

Patrick Mahomes, Chiefs - Right Elbow

Mahomes is expected to practice in full Wednesday ahead of Sunday's Week 10 matchup against the Falcons, according to Chiefs head coach Andy Reid. The quarterback suffered a right elbow injury during Sunday's Week 9 victory over the Jets, but an MRI revealed no major structural damage. Mahomes told reporters the injury is now a matter of pain management and is expected to play Sunday.

OUT/IR

Josh Jacobs, Packers - Fractured Ring Finger (OUT Week 10)

Jacobs is expected to undergo surgery later this week to repair a fractured ring finger suffered during Sunday's Week 9 game against the Patriots. The Packers running back has been ruled out for Sunday's Week 10 matchup against the Vikings but could return within two to three weeks, according to reports. Green Bay will decide Saturday whether to place Jacobs on injured reserve, although an IR designation is not guaranteed. The Packers have a Week 11 bye, potentially giving Jacobs an opportunity to return in Week 12.

Malik Willis, Dolphins - Groin (Injured Reserve)

The Dolphins placed Willis on injured reserve Tuesday due to a groin injury, sidelining their starting quarterback for at least four games. Willis had received treatment for the injury over the past two weeks but had not missed practice or game action before Miami's decision to place him on IR.

text:
Los Angeles Rams star wide receiver Puka Nacua is expected to be placed on the injured reserve list list after the knee injuries he suffered in the game against the Washington Commanders this past weekend.

If Nacua does get an IR designation, he will have to miss at least four games with a potential to miss even more time.

This is bad news for the Rams. It would be even worse if Nacua’s season was over.

But, ESPN NFL insider Dan Graziano reported that this is unlikely in an article that was published on Wednesday.

“Rams coach Sean McVay said Monday that Nacua was likely to land on injured reserve because of knee and toe injuries, but so far he has not. If the Rams put him on IR, the soonest he could return is Week 15 against the Cowboys,” Graziano wrote.

“If they think it’s possible Nacua might only have to miss four weeks, they could refrain from putting him on IR and possibly have him back in time for their Week 14 game at San Francisco.

“This all becomes moot if they put Nacua on IR this week, but just keep an eye on the situation if they don’t,” he continued.

“Speaking to people close to this situation Monday evening, they were very adamant that Nacua’s injury isn’t season-ending and that they hope to get him back for Week 14 or 15.”

Graziano’s report that those close to the situation are “adamant” Nacua’s season isn’t over offers Rams fans a much-needed reason for optimism.

text:
The Detroit Lions (6-2) head to Germany in Week 10 to take on the New England Patriots (5-4), but before they travel overseas, they’ll hold two practices in Allen Park: a walkthrough on Wednesday and a standard practice on Thursday.

A walkthrough practice means that all participation levels are estimates from the coaching staff based on how the player would have participated in a traditional practice. So, with that in mind, let’s look at Wednesday’s injury report and get you up to date on what we know.

Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded.

RB Isiah Pacheco (MCL/Back, IR) — expected to be out until December

OL Giovanni Manu (undisclosed, NFI) — eligible to begin practicing at any time

OL Ben Bartch (foot, IR) — eligible to begin practicing at any time

LB Devin White (forearm, IR) — eligible to begin practicing at any time

LB Jack Campbell (neck, IR) — determined to play football again

S Kerby Joseph (knee, PUP) — injury evaluation clock started

S Thomas Harper (ankle, IR) — eligible to begin practicing at any time

Campbell was officially added to the Lions injured reserve list last Saturday, and while he continues to improve, his overall health and status with the team remain undetermined. That said, Campbell is reportedly determined to play football again and wants the team to “make sure the house is taken care of until [he] can get back.”

Estimated no practice

RB Sione Vaki (ankle) — downgraded to no practice

C Cade Mays (low ankle sprain)

CB D.J. Reed (hip)

Vaki popped up on Week 9’s injury report late in the week, and while he was given a questionable designation for the game, he was available and contributed in RB2 and starting special teams roles. The Lions may take things slowly with him this week, but unless he had a set back, he still has a chance to play in Germany.

Mays and Reed were both injured in Week 8, missed Week 9, and appear to be longshots to suit up in Week 10, according to Lions coach Dan Campbell.

“I don’t see Cade and Reed practicing today,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said on Wednesday. “I don’t see them practicing today. They have got a way outside shot of playing. Way, way, way outside shot.”

Juice Scruggs has been starting at center while Mays recovers, and the Lions have rotated corners to split snaps while Reed is sidelined. Last week, Rock Ya-Sin got the start and played the majority of the rotation, but Khalil Dorsey, Ennis Rakestraw, and recently promoted Nick Whiteside saw some situational work as well.

Estimated limited practice

QB Jared Goff (chest) — New Injury

WR Amon-Ra St. Brown (rib)

S Brian Branch (hip) — New Injury

S Kerby Joseph (knee, PUP) — Days remaining in injury evaluation clock: 6

Goff took a few more shots against the Dolphins than he normally does, so this could be a light day for him to recover, as there have been no indicators that they’re worried about him missing this game. We’ll still have to wait until Thursday to get a better idea, but there’s no need to panic just yet.

St. Brown was injured in Week 8 and had limited practice time ahead of Week 9, but he didn’t appear limited in the game. With this week’s game in his mother’s home country, and all the charity work he’s done in Germany over the last two years, you can be sure he’s playing.

Branch just cleared the NFL’s concussion protocol only to show up on this week’s injury report with a new ailment. It’s not clear when he suffered this hip injury, as he played the entire game last Sunday, but like Goff, we’ll have to double check his status on Thursday before we can feel totally comfortable.

Joseph continues to make positive strides as he acclimates back to football, and the Lions are happy with his progress, but Campbell has already told the media that Joseph won’t play in Germany. The Lions don’t have to decide on his PUP status until next Tuesday.

Estimated full practice

RB Jacob Saylors (neck/hamstring) — Upgraded after limited practice last week

EDGE DJ Wonnum (concussion) — Upgraded after no practice last week

Saylors injured his neck in Week 7, couldn’t play the entire game in Week 8, and fully missed Week 9, even though he was a limited participant, he’s now added a hamstring injury to his list of ailments. Getting more work this week is positive, and despite the full practice, the Lions will probably take it slow with him.

Wonnum suffered a concussion in Week 8 that kept him from playing in Week 9, but he’s made progress since then and is close to completing the NFL’s concussion protocols, according to Campbell:

“Wonnum, he’s cleared his first obstacle; second obstacle here. So, he’s going to be able to practice today. As long as he gets through practice, he should be good to go. So, that’s encouraging.”

No longer on the injury report

LB Amen Ogbongbemiga (toe)

CB Rock Ya-Sin (cramps)

The players listed in this section no longer require a spot on the injury report.

Patriots’ initial injury report

Coming soon.

title: NFL Injury Report: Puka Nacua's Return Uncertain, Mahomes Likely to Play Through Injury And More
